title: Vectorize/parallelize the CPU-bound per-position signal computation loop (kangaroo_tail and friends)
description:
backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups's own investigation (see its `decisions` entry) re-confirmed PR #352's review finding: for a realistic full-history daily series (e.g. AAPL's ~11,539-row/~46-year cached history), `app.signals.kangaroo_tail.detect_kangaroo_tails` alone costs ~1.7-1.8s per ticker (independently re-measured here via `cProfile`, matching the parent task's own ~1.7s/ticker figure) -- dominated by `_evaluate_candidate`'s per-bar Python loop, which re-slices a `lookback`-row window and re-runs `.mean()`/`.max()`/`.min()`/multiple `.iloc[...]` scalar lookups on every one of the ~11,528 bars scanned, rather than doing a single vectorized pass over the whole series. `app.signals.divergence.find_divergences`/`app.signals.swing_points.find_swing_points` are a smaller but real secondary cost over the same full-history frame (not re-profiled in detail by this task's own investigation -- left for whoever picks this up).

This is the CPU-bound bottleneck backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups's own investigation concluded is now the DOMINANT cost of a realistic swing-mode portfolio load (its own `decisions` entry has the full comparison against the now-concurrent, comparatively cheap ~2.7s-combined provider-fetch phase PR #352 already fixed) -- fixing the provider-round-trip side of this problem (PR #352, and this task's own two-phase `GET /api/portfolio/risk` fix) does NOT address it, so the original 'first load is very very slow' user complaint is likely only partially resolved until this CPU-bound side is also tackled, for any portfolio holding one or more long-history tickers.

**A vectorized rewrite is very likely feasible and worth doing**: backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups's own investigation prototyped (not shipped -- see that task's `decisions` entry for the exact approach: `pandas.Series.shift`/`.rolling(lookback)` replacing the per-bar window slice, `np.where` replacing the per-bar direction/retracement branching) a vectorized equivalent of `detect_kangaroo_tails`'s full algorithm and measured it against the SAME synthetic ~11,539-row fixture the CPU-bound profiling used: identical tail set (60/60 matching `(date, direction)` pairs) at ~450x wall-clock speedup (1.80s -> 0.004s). This is strong evidence the rewrite is algorithmically sound, but was deliberately NOT shipped by that task -- see its own `decisions` entry for why (needs this task's own dedicated hand-computed reference-value tests per the `add-indicator` convention, not just 'matches the old implementation on one synthetic fixture', plus the same `verify-elder-signal`-governed scrutiny `backend-kangaroo-tail-pattern`'s original implementation got, given this directly gates SELL/BUY confidence).

**Two independent, non-exclusive angles to weigh** (this task's own checklist should decide between them, or do both):
1. **Algorithmic**: vectorize `detect_kangaroo_tails` (and, time permitting, profile then similarly vectorize `find_divergences`/`find_swing_points`'s own whole-history passes if they turn out to be a comparable cost) -- the higher-payoff fix (a ~450x measured speedup on the single function profiled so far), but higher-risk: it touches core signal-detection math directly, and needs the same reference-value rigor as any other indicator/signal change in this codebase.
2. **Infra/parallelization**: parallelize `get_portfolio`/`get_risk`'s own per-position `analyse()` calls across positions. Explicitly NOT a `ThreadPoolExecutor` job like this task's own I/O-bound provider-fetch fixes (PR #352, backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups) -- `analyse()` is CPU-bound Python (GIL-bound), so a thread pool wouldn't parallelize it at all. Would need a `ProcessPoolExecutor` (with its own overhead: pickling each position's OHLCV frames across the process boundary, worker startup cost) or an out-of-process task queue -- a materially different, heavier concurrency mechanism than anything currently in this codebase's `app/api/` layer, so a fresh design/cost-benefit pass is warranted before committing to it, not an assumed drop-in.

checklist.step: Decide (and record as a `decisions` entry) which of the two angles above to pursue first (or both), with real weighing of effort/risk/payoff -- e.g. the algorithmic vectorization already has strong prototype evidence (450x on the one function profiled) and doesn't need a new concurrency mechanism, but touches core signal math; the ProcessPoolExecutor angle is more contained (no signal-math changes) but adds a new, heavier concurrency primitive and its own overhead that could eat into the gain at today's typical portfolio sizes.

If pursuing the algorithmic angle: rewrite `detect_kangaroo_tails` as a vectorized pandas/numpy implementation (backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups's own `decisions` entry has a working prototype approach to start from -- shift/rolling for the baseline-range window, np.where for direction/retracement branching), with hand-computed reference-value tests matching this codebase's `add-indicator` convention (not just parity-against-old-implementation on a synthetic fixture) -- verify against `docs/ideas.md`'s own worked description and `backend-kangaroo-tail-pattern.json`'s original decisions for every threshold/tie-break (including the up-priority outside-bar tie-break `backend-kangaroo-tail-pattern-followups.json` documents) so behavior genuinely matches the book-derived algorithm, not just the old code's own possibly-already-subtly-wrong output. Get `verify-elder-signal` review before merging, given this gates SELL/BUY confidence.

If time/scope permits: profile `find_divergences`/`find_swing_points` the same way (cProfile against a realistic full-history frame) to confirm whether they're worth the same vectorization treatment, or whether kangaroo_tail alone was the dominant secondary cost.

If pursuing the parallelization angle instead of (or alongside) vectorization: design and implement a `ProcessPoolExecutor`-based (or equivalent) concurrent per-position `analyse()` fan-out for `GET /api/portfolio` and `GET /api/portfolio/risk`, with a measured before/after comparison (not assumed) accounting for process-pool startup/pickling overhead at realistic portfolio sizes, and a genuinely discriminating concurrency-correctness test per this codebase's established mutation-testing standard.

Re-measure the full swing-mode portfolio load (mirroring backend-portfolio-load-performance's own timing methodology) after whichever fix(es) are implemented, and record the before/after numbers in a `decisions` entry -- this is the task that actually closes out the original 'first load is very very slow' user complaint's CPU-bound half, so its own claim of having done so should be measured, not assumed.

PR #353 review finding (backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups, non-blocking): `_fetch_weekly_ohlcv_concurrently`'s own docstring (`backend/app/api/routers/portfolio.py`) claims 'A duplicate ticker in `tickers` (two positions on the same ticker) is fetched at most once -- the returned dict is keyed by ticker'. This is inaccurate: `{ticker: executor.submit(_fetch, ticker) for ticker in tickers}` calls `executor.submit` (and therefore `_fetch`/`provider.get_weekly_ohlcv`) once per *occurrence* of a ticker in the list, not once per distinct ticker -- only the *stored future* per key ends up deduplicated to the last submission (verified independently: a 3-item list with one repeated ticker produced 3 calls to the wrapped function, not 2). This exact behavior is pre-existing (inherited unchanged from `_prefetch_swing_weekly_ohlcv`'s own prior inline `ThreadPoolExecutor` code, which never made this claim), and is currently unreachable in practice since `PositionORM.ticker` has a DB-level `unique=True` constraint (no two positions can share a ticker today, per `app/db/models.py`'s own multi-lot-support comment) -- so no live portfolio can actually trigger a duplicate-ticker call. Still worth fixing before any future multi-lot-support work makes the scenario reachable: either correct the docstring's claim (say it dedupes the *result*, not the *fetch*), or actually dedupe `tickers` before submitting (e.g. `list(dict.fromkeys(tickers))`) so the code matches what the docstring already asserts.

decisions.decision: Chose the ALGORITHMIC angle (vectorize `detect_kangaroo_tails`) over the `ProcessPoolExecutor`-based per-position-parallelization angle, and did not pursue the latter at all in this task.
decisions.rationale: Weighing effort/risk/payoff as the checklist asks: the algorithmic angle already had strong prototype evidence from the parent task (450x measured speedup, 60/60 tail parity on a synthetic fixture) and needs no new concurrency primitive anywhere in this codebase's `app/api/` layer -- the risk is entirely contained to one already-well-isolated, already-heavily-documented pure function with an existing hand-computed reference-value test suite to verify against. The `ProcessPoolExecutor` angle, by contrast, would add a genuinely new, heavier concurrency mechanism (pickling each position's full OHLCV DataFrame across a process boundary, worker pool startup cost) that this task's own description flags as needing its own fresh design/cost-benefit pass, with a real risk the pickling/startup overhead eats into the gain at today's typical portfolio sizes (a handful to a few dozen positions, not hundreds) -- and it wouldn't reduce the actual per-ticker CPU cost at all, only try to run several full-cost computations concurrently across cores. Since the algorithmic fix directly attacks the measured dominant cost (detect_kangaroo_tails' O(n) per-bar loop) with a large, already-demonstrated speedup and doesn't preclude parallelization being added later on top of the now-much-cheaper per-position cost if ever needed, it was the clearly higher-payoff, lower-risk choice to pursue first. Not ruled out for a future task if per-position parallelization is ever still wanted after this fix -- just not needed to resolve the specific bottleneck this task was filed to address.

decisions.decision:
Rewrote `app.signals.kangaroo_tail.detect_kangaroo_tails` as a single vectorized pandas/numpy pass (rolling `.mean()`/`.max()`/`.min()` each `.shift(1)`-ed for the baseline-range/window-extreme checks, `.shift(1)`/`.shift(-1)` for the flanking bars' ranges and the confirming bar's close, `np.where` for the up/down-direction branching in the body-retracement and confirms-direction checks, one final `&`-combined boolean mask), replacing the old per-bar Python loop (`_evaluate_candidate`, called once per candidate position). Every one of the module's own documented 5 algorithm steps (baseline window, tail qualification incl. the up-priority outside-bar tie-break, body retracement, flanking-bar normality against the SAME baseline as the candidate -- not a baseline recomputed for the flank's own position, confirming-bar direction) and the suggested-stop formula were preserved bit-for-bit in intent, not just approximately -- see the module's own updated docstring ('Vectorized implementation' section) for the full mapping from old per-bar operation to new vectorized one.

Verification (per the add-indicator convention -- hand-computed reference values, not just old-vs-new parity): (1) ALL 25 pre-existing hand-computed reference-value tests in `tests/unit/signals/test_kangaroo_tail.py` (written against the OLD per-bar implementation, using a flat, hand-computable filler baseline per that file's own docstring) pass UNCHANGED against the new vectorized implementation -- these tests assert exact hand-derived field values (range_multiple, suggested_stop, direction, dates), not just 'a KangarooTail was returned', so this alone is genuine reference-value verification, not parity-only. (2) Added one new test (`TestMultipleTailsInOneScan`) exercising a vectorized-rewrite-specific risk not covered by any existing test: `detect_kangaroo_tails` (not just `latest_kangaroo_tail`) correctly returning MULTIPLE simultaneously-qualifying positions from one array pass with each tail's own fields correctly attributed (not mixed up via an off-by-one in the `np.flatnonzero` position-to-fields mapping) -- both tails' every field independently hand-verified. 100% line/branch coverage on the rewritten module (`pytest --cov=app.signals.kangaroo_tail`). (3) Additionally cross-checked old-vs-new on two large-scale synthetic ~11,539-row (AAPL-scale) fixtures for extra confidence beyond the hand-computed suite: a random-walk fixture (0 tails, confirming no spurious detections) and a purpose-built fixture with 460 engineered candidate patterns injected every ~25 bars (10 of which pass every gate) -- EVERY field of every returned `KangarooTail` matched exactly (not just the count) between the old scalar implementation (retrieved via `git show origin/main:...` for comparison purposes only, not shipped) and the new vectorized one. (4) Manually mutation-tested the up-priority outside-bar tie-break (`direction_is_up = makes_new_high` -> `makes_new_low`) and confirmed 8 of the 26 tests failed as expected, then reverted -- proving the test suite actually discriminates that specific behavior, not just passing coincidentally. (5) Applied `verify-elder-signal`'s own checklist methodology directly (docs/Analyse.md Row 13, lines 168-178): walked every one of the doc's 5 numbered steps against the new vectorized code side-by-side and confirmed no drift -- kangaroo_tail remains 'detection + exposure only' (not wired into `_determine_signal`/Impulse gate/confidence scoring, unchanged by this task, per docs/Analyse.md's own explicit statement of that scope). ruff and mypy both clean on the rewritten module.

One narrow, judged-negligible theoretical precision caveat: `pandas.Series.rolling(lookback).mean()` computes an incremental (add-newest/subtract-oldest) running sum internally, which could in principle produce a floating-point result differing in the last few bits from the old code's fresh `.mean()` recomputed on each window slice, in a case where a bar's range sits EXACTLY on the `range_multiplier` threshold boundary. Not observed in either large-scale empirical parity check above (zero divergence across 460 injected + a full random-walk series), and the old scalar implementation's own `>=` threshold comparison was already exposed to the identical category of floating-point-exactness sensitivity (any two implementations of the same formula in different order can disagree in the last ULP at an exact boundary) -- judged not a new risk this rewrite introduces, just the same pre-existing float-comparison caveat inherent to any threshold-based numeric check, consistent with this codebase's own universal `pytest.approx`-based tolerance convention elsewhere.
decisions.rationale: The checklist explicitly requires hand-computed reference-value tests per the add-indicator convention, not just 'matches old implementation on one synthetic fixture' (the exact gap the parent task's own prototype was blocked on shipping) -- reusing the pre-existing reference-value suite unchanged, adding one new reference-value test for the rewrite's own specific new risk (multi-tail-per-scan field attribution), and independently applying verify-elder-signal's own methodology directly (rather than only trusting the prototype's own self-consistency framing) satisfies that bar. The large-fixture parity checks are kept only as SUPPLEMENTARY evidence, not the primary verification method, precisely because the task description called out that they alone wouldn't have caught a bug present in both implementations -- the hand-computed suite is what actually rules that out, since it was derived independently from the book's algorithm description, not from either code path.

decisions.decision:
Profiled `app.signals.divergence.find_divergences`/`app.signals.swing_points.find_swing_points` against the same synthetic ~11,539-row (AAPL-scale) daily series used for the kangaroo_tail re-profiling, to confirm (per checklist item 3, 'if time/scope permits') whether either is a comparable secondary cost worth the same vectorization treatment. Findings: `find_swing_points` (one full-history call) measured ~0.09s -- already effectively vectorized (`app.signals._swing_extremes.rolling_extreme_masks`, itself built by `backend-swing-point-detector-followups`), not worth further work. `find_divergences` measured ~0.72s for the SIX full-history swing-point scans `current_divergence`'s own per-indicator-per-kind fan-out actually performs in production (macd_histogram/stochastic/rsi x bullish/bearish) -- each individual `find_divergences` call re-runs `find_swing_points` fresh (`find_divergences`'s own docstring already flags this: 'fine for a single whole-history pass... but a caller re-running this once per bar... should use build_divergence_swing_cache' -- that caching advice is about the PER-BAR incremental-walk case, not this redundant-across-indicators case, which is a distinct, smaller inefficiency `current_divergence` itself has: 3 indicators x 2 kinds each independently re-deriving PRICE's own swing points from the exact same `price` series, when the swing-point pass only actually depends on `price`, not on which indicator/kind is being evaluated). Both are meaningfully smaller than kangaroo_tail's original ~1.6-1.8s cost, and divergence's ~0.72s (now the largest remaining O(history)-ish secondary cost after this task's kangaroo_tail fix) is driven by genuine redundant computation, not an algorithmically-inefficient single pass the way the old kangaroo_tail loop was.

Did NOT implement a fix for this redundancy in this task -- judged out of this task's own scope (which was filed specifically for kangaroo_tail's already-confirmed-dominant cost, not a general audit of every O(history) signal-engine cost) and it would mean touching `app.signals.divergence.current_divergence`'s own call structure (a `build_divergence_swing_cache`-equivalent single swing-point pass shared across all 3 indicators, reusable for `current_divergence` the same way it's already reused for `confirmed_divergence_as_of`) -- additional core-signal-detection-adjacent surface area beyond what this task's own checklist scoped, without its own dedicated hand-computed reference-value verification pass. Left as a documented finding here rather than filed as a new tracked follow-up task, since checklist item 3 explicitly frames this as optional ('if time/scope permits') rather than a required deliverable, and the actual required work (checklist items 1-2, 4-6) is what this task exists to close out.
decisions.rationale: Genuinely measuring rather than assuming resolves checklist item 3 with real numbers instead of a guess, per this task's own established convention (backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups's own re-profiling of PR #352's claim). Not implementing a fix here keeps this task's own scope bounded to what it was actually filed for (kangaroo_tail, per its own title and description's dominant-cost framing) rather than open-endedly expanding into every O(history) cost this investigation happens to surface -- consistent with how the parent task itself handled discovering the vectorization opportunity (documented + filed as its own task, rather than silently expanded into).

decisions.decision:
Re-measured the full swing-mode `GET /api/portfolio` load (mirroring backend-portfolio-load-performance's own TestClient-based timing methodology) before vs after this task's kangaroo_tail vectorization, using a local no-network stub `DataProvider` serving a realistic ~11,539-row (AAPL-scale) daily history to N=8 swing-mode positions (isolating the CPU-bound signal-computation cost this task targets from provider-fetch latency, which PR #352/backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups already made concurrent/fast). Measured (3-run average each, after a discarded warm-up call): BEFORE (old per-bar kangaroo_tail loop, monkeypatched back in via a copy of the pre-vectorization implementation retrieved from `git show origin/main:...` for measurement purposes only) ~20.52s; AFTER (this task's vectorized implementation) ~6.11s -- a measured ~3.36x end-to-end speedup for this realistic multi-long-history-ticker portfolio load.

This is a genuine, substantial improvement to the CPU-bound half of the original 'first load is very very slow' complaint this whole task chain traces back to, but does NOT fully close it out: ~6.11s for 8 positions (~0.76s/position) still reflects real remaining CPU-bound cost from `analyse()`'s other whole-history computations (EMA/MACD/Stochastic/RSI series computation, `find_divergences`' own ~0.72s/ticker redundant-swing-scan cost identified above, support/resistance zone detection, etc.) -- none of which this task's own checklist scoped it to address. A portfolio with many long-history positions will still see a multi-second load, just roughly a third of what it was before this fix, not reduced to negligible.
decisions.rationale: Checklist item 5 explicitly asks this claim be measured, not assumed, mirroring the same standard backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups already held PR #352's own claims to (independently re-profiling rather than trusting a prior figure). Reporting the full, honest picture (a real 3.36x improvement, but not a full resolution of the underlying complaint) rather than only the isolated kangaroo_tail-function speedup (which alone would overstate the end-to-end user-facing benefit) follows that same standard -- the isolated function speedup (~955x/~765x) and the end-to-end portfolio-load speedup (~3.36x) are both true and both worth recording, but they answer different questions, and conflating them would be misleading about what a user actually experiences.

decisions.decision: Fixed `_fetch_weekly_ohlcv_concurrently`'s behavior (deduplicating `tickers` via `list(dict.fromkeys(tickers))` before any `executor.submit` call) rather than only correcting its docstring's inaccurate 'fetched at most once' claim (PR #353 review finding).
decisions.rationale: The docstring's existing claim is the semantically RIGHT contract for this function to have (a caller shouldn't need to pre-deduplicate its own ticker list, and `weekly_by_id`'s per-position keying at each call site already assumes exactly this) -- weakening the docstring to describe the buggy behavior accurately would be technically honest but would leave a real latent inefficiency (and, if `PositionORM.ticker`'s DB-level `unique=True` constraint is ever relaxed for genuine multi-lot support, a real *correctness* risk: a duplicate ticker's SECOND submission's future would silently overwrite the first's in the `futures` dict, so if the two fetches raced and gave different transient results -- e.g. one hit a rate limit, one didn't -- which result 'wins' would depend on dict-overwrite order, not on which was actually correct) sitting behind an accurate-but-weaker docstring instead of fixed. The one-line `list(dict.fromkeys(...))` fix (order-preserving, no new dependency) is strictly cheaper than the redundant round trip(s) it prevents even in the common single-fetch case, so there's no performance tradeoff being made against fixing it. Verified with a genuinely discriminating unit test (`tests/integration/test_portfolio_get.py::TestFetchWeeklyOhlcvConcurrentlyDedup`) calling the private helper directly with a duplicate-ticker list (since this scenario is currently unreachable end-to-end through `GET /api/portfolio` given the DB unique constraint) -- manually mutation-tested by reverting the fix and confirming the new test fails (3 calls instead of 2), then re-applied and confirmed it passes.
